topic: understanding the concept of the pigeonhole principle in combinatorics

easy.text: The pigeonhole principle states that if you have more items than containers, then:

options.text: At least one container must hold more than one item
options.feedback: Correct -- this simple but powerful principle guarantees at least one 'overloaded' container whenever items outnumber containers.

options.text: Every container must hold exactly the same number of items
options.feedback: This isn't what the principle guarantees -- it only guarantees that AT LEAST ONE container has more than one item, not that all containers have equal amounts.

options.text: Some containers must remain completely empty
options.feedback: This isn't necessarily guaranteed by the pigeonhole principle -- it specifically only guarantees that at least one container is 'overloaded' (has more than one item), not that others must be empty.

options.text: It is impossible to distribute the items among the containers at all
options.feedback: This isn't accurate -- distribution IS possible; the pigeonhole principle specifically guarantees a certain OUTCOME of that distribution (at least one overloaded container), not that distribution itself is impossible.

medium.text: In a room of 13 people, why must at least two people share the same birth MONTH (ignoring year), according to the pigeonhole principle?

options.text: Since there are only 12 possible birth months (containers) but 13 people (items), at least one month must contain 2 or more people
options.feedback: Correct -- with 13 items (people) needing to fit into only 12 containers (months), the pigeonhole principle guarantees at least one month must be shared by at least two people.

options.text: This is actually just a coincidence with no real mathematical guarantee behind it
options.feedback: This isn't accurate -- this IS mathematically guaranteed by the pigeonhole principle, not merely coincidental, given that there are more people (13) than available months (12).

options.text: This would only be true if there were exactly 12 people, not 13
options.feedback: This isn't accurate -- the guarantee specifically requires MORE items than containers (13 people > 12 months), which is precisely why 13 (not exactly 12) people guarantees this outcome.

options.text: The number of possible birth months has no actual connection to this guarantee
options.feedback: This isn't accurate -- the number of possible birth months (12, serving as the 'containers') is DIRECTLY and centrally connected to and is precisely why this specific guarantee holds when there are 13 people.

hard.text: A more advanced ('generalized') version of the pigeonhole principle states that if you distribute N items into K containers, at least one container must hold AT LEAST ⌈N/K⌉ items (the ceiling/rounded-up value of N divided by K). Using this generalized version, if 50 students are distributed among 8 classrooms, what is the minimum number of students guaranteed to be in at least one classroom?

options.feedback: Correct -- since 50÷8=6.25, and we must round UP (ceiling function) for this guarantee, at least one classroom must contain at least 7 students.

This doesn't correctly apply the CEILING (round-up) function required by the generalized pigeonhole principle -- simply rounding down (or truncating) 6.25 to 6 isn't mathematically correct for this guarantee.
This is just the total number of students, not the correctly calculated minimum guaranteed number in any single classroom based on the generalized principle.
This is just the total number of classrooms, not the correctly calculated minimum guaranteed number of students in any single classroom.

easy.hard: This principle guarantees that distributing a set exceeding a given container count necessitates at least one container accommodating multiple set elements.
easy.medium: If you have more things than boxes to put them in, at least one box has to end up with more than one thing.
easy.easy: If you have more things than boxes, at least one box ends up with more than one thing.

medium.hard: Compare the total item count against the total available distinct container count to determine whether the basic pigeonhole guarantee applies.
medium.medium: Count how many possible months there are (12) versus how many people there are (13) -- since people outnumber months, someone has to share.
medium.easy: There are 12 months but 13 people, so at least two people must share a month.

hard.hard: Apply the generalized pigeonhole formula by dividing the total item count by the total container count, then round the result up to the nearest whole number.
hard.medium: Divide 50 by 8 to get 6.25, then round UP to the next whole number since you can't have a fraction of a student.
hard.easy: 50 divided by 8 is 6.25, rounded up to 7.
